did_you_know.text: Did you know? This chapter describes a messenger who prepares the way before the Lord comes to His temple; he is also called “the messenger of the covenant.”
Did you know? The Lord’s coming is described as an overwhelming process: He is compared to a refiner’s fire and a launderer’s soap.
Did you know? The purification focuses especially on the descendants of Levi, so that their service as those who present offerings may be proper and righteous before the Lord.
Did you know? The divine judgment in this chapter includes not only religious sinners, but also sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and those who oppress hired workers, widows, orphans, and foreigners.
Did you know? The prophet presents the Lord’s unchanging nature as the reason the descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed, even though they have sinned.
Did you know? The call, “Return to me, and I will return to you,” presents repentance as a step toward mutual closeness between the people and the Lord.
Did you know? In this chapter, withholding the tithe and the offering is described as robbing the Lord, because they are intended for the treasury and the temple service.
Did you know? The Lord calls His people to bring the entire tithe to the treasury and describes the blessing as opening the windows of heaven and pouring out blessing without measure.
Did you know? The words of those who fear the Lord to one another are described as so significant that a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who think about His name.
Did you know? At the end of the book, the prophet Elijah is promised to be sent before the great and awesome day of the Lord, to turn the hearts of parents to their children and prepare the people.
